newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon announces delay in chemical study.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon announces delay in chemical study.

text.p: Announcing a delay in CIA efforts to help solve a major medical mystery, the Pentagon said on Thursday it may never know how many thousands of Gulf War troops might have been exposed to Iraqi chemical agents.

But Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon denied any political motive in a decision by the Central Intelligence Agency and the Pentagon to have private experts review a new CIA study of a cloud of sarin nerve gas from the 1991 destruction of an Iraqi ammunition dump.
The review could delay the release of the spy agency's "model" of the wind-blown cloud from the Kamisiyah dump in southern Iraq until after the Nov. 5 presidential election.

"The reason there is no political connection is it will not help us to delay this," Bacon said when asked by reporters if there was an attempt to put off bad news on President Bill Clinton's behalf in a growing controversy.

The Defence Department this month said at least 15,000 and perhaps far more U.S. Gulf War troops might have been exposed to sarin when Kamisiyah was destroyed by U.S. military engineers. Published reports have suggested the figure could reach 100,000 U.S. troops from several divisions.

"I think it is important to realise that we will never have a precise, definitive picture of how chemical agents may have been dispersed on March 10, 1991, from Kamisiyah," Bacon said in a pessimistic assessment on Thursday.

"It is impossible to go back and reconstruct precise wind patterns. It's impossible for us even to know how many weapons were exploded, how many jumped out of the pit, how many of them propelled themselves into the sand and buried themselves, how may didn't explode at all."

The issue, in which the Pentagon has denied ignoring complaints ranging from numbness to loss of memory from as many as 60,000 Gulf War veterans or trying to cover up information, has become a major controversy.

The CIA, using weather patterns and other information, has been working in recent weeks to develop a "model" of the cloud that drifted from the dump and how it was influenced by weather and other factors.

"I would say he (CIA Director John Deutch) wants these results to be as well-reviewed as possible and he has set up a programme to do that," Bacon said of a "peer review" panel of experts who will look at the study. He said the panel had not yet been named and could take weeks to review the CIA model.
The Defence Department said no deaths have been caused by chemical agents and it has been unable to find any illnesses caused by such agents or any common cause of so-called "Gulf War Syndrome."
The U.S. government, on orders from Clinton, last year mounted a major effort to resolve Gulf War medical complaints.
